DBS, OCBC, UOB: Singapore Banks Are Cheaper, But Are They a Bargain?
article:
Earlier this month, Citi downgraded
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, from Neutral to Sell, with a target price of S$27.50.
In response, investors hit the sell button.
OCBC shares tumbled 5.9% in a single session.
DBS Group
(SGX: D05) and
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11), or UOB, slid alongside it.
The message was simple: sell OCBC.
But here’s what most investors missed.
Divide Citi’s target price by OCBC’s book value (as at 30 June 2026) of S$13.73 per share, and you get a surprising ratio: two times book.
Let me put that in perspective.
Over the past decade, OCBC shares have traded at an average of 1.22 times book value.
Between 2017 and 2025, the ratio was below 1.5 times most of the time.
In other words, Citi’s bearish target still values OCBC at more than 60% above its long-term average multiple.
Not long ago, a target like that would have read as wildly optimistic.
So if even the Sell call looks expensive by historical standards, what does that tell you about Singapore’s banks today?
The answer is: bank shares are indeed cheaper.
But they are still not cheap.
A lower share price does not make a bargain.
When shares are trading at higher multiples, the banks have more to live up to.
And that hasn’t changed.

Source: Company filings, Fiscal.ai, author’s calculations. Based on OCBC’s share price of S$29.00 as at 16 October 2026 and book value of S$13.73 as at 30 June 2026. The current yield includes OCBC’s special dividend; the figure in brackets excludes it.
OCBC, even after its recent tumble, sits at about 2.1 times book.
That’s over 70% above its long-term average.
For most of the past decade, OCBC traded close to its average, marked by the dashed red line.
That changed from late 2024 onwards, when the shares broke well clear of their historical range.
Notice the deep dip in 2020 as well.
The dividend yield points the same way.
At S$29, OCBC yields 3.6%, below its 10-year average of 4.5%.
But that figure includes a special dividend.
Count only the ordinary dividend, and the yield falls to 3.1%.
Even at Citi’s S$27.50 target, OCBC would yield 3.8%, still below its long-term average.
The price of a bargain
For a bank to trade at a truly cheap valuation, there’s a trade-off you have to accept.
Something bad usually has to happen first.
If you’re a deep value investor, you would wait for OCBC to trade at or below its book value of S$13.73.
But you won’t know when that will be.
It has happened only around three times in the past 20 years.
The sharpest dip of the past decade came during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
That’s the dip you saw in the chart earlier.
Related articles:

Get Smart: Optimise for a calm mind
Let’s return to where we started.
Citi’s Sell call on OCBC sent the shares tumbling.
Yet behind the headline was a model whose target still valued OCBC at two times book.
If you sold on the headline alone, you acted on someone else’s assumptions.
Here’s what I’d suggest instead.
First, know what you’re paying for.
At today’s prices, there’s still a fair bit of optimism built into bank shares.
In other words, the business has to live up to it.
Second, decide what kind of investor you are, then work out your price from there.
A deep value investor, an income investor, and an analyst can all arrive at different prices for the same bank.
And finally, do not optimise for performance.
Optimise for a calm mind.
Genuinely cheap bank shares only show up when the news is frightening.
When that day comes again, as it did in March 2020, a calm mind is the best strategy you can have.

title: China’s growth rebound tops forecasts to close in on target
article:
(Oct 19): China’s growth accelerated more than expected in the third quarter, boosting the odds of the economy reaching Beijing’s annual target and dimming the prospects for additional easing measures.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.5% from a year ago after a gain of 4.3% in the second quarter, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Monday, compared with the median forecast of 4.4% by economists surveyed by Bloomberg. That took expansion in the first nine months of the year to 4.6% — within the government’s annual goal of 4.5%-5%.

The improvement in the economy should give policymakers some breathing room, allowing them to hold off on further easing as they remain constrained by thin bank margins and persistent fiscal strain on local governments.

Industrial production growth accelerated to 5.5% on year in September, matching forecasts. Fixed-asset investment shrank 7.2% in the first nine months of the year, unchanged from its drop in January-August.

Retail sales picked up far more than expected to 1.1%, versus a 0.4% rise in August. Excluding car purchases, retail sales grew 3.9% from a year ago, the fastest pace since October 2025.

See also: Chinese stocks turn biggest losers as global AI trade stumbles

“Bigger fiscal spending helped both fixed-asset investment and retail sales,” said Xing Zhaopeng, senior China strategist at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. “The recovery remains unsolid because the fiscal outlook is not stable. The question will be how much fiscal expansion can do in the future. We still see a downside risk to 2027.”

The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds climbed one basis point to 1.65% after the data release. The yuan held on to its earlier gain, rising 0.1% to 6.6829 per dollar in offshore trading.

China’s currency has advanced over 4% against the greenback since the start of the year to outperform most of its Asian peers, thanks to rising exports and the central bank’s tolerance for a stronger exchange rate.

See also: China plans AI tech export curbs to manage security risks

With industrial output growing at the fastest since March in a sign of China’s supply-side “strength,” the government’s support for the economy will likely “stay at the current level with only a marginal adjustment,” said Helen Qiao, chief economist for greater China at BofA Global Research.

Even as the slowdown intensified in recent months, officials initially focused on implementing existing pro-growth policies, before dialing up their support three weeks ago with a package of fresh targeted measures.

Growth in the world’s second-largest economy has been marked by a divide between booming exports — stoked by a global investment supercycle in artificial intelligence — and sluggish household spending, with investment stuck in a long slump. The job market has also softened while a years-long property downturn drags on.

Property investment plunged 20.6% in the first nine months and capital spending on infrastructure slumped 4.2%, a deterioration from their performance in January-August. The surveyed urban jobless rate unexpectedly improved to 5.2% in September from 5.3% in the prior month.

Frail domestic demand has left China increasingly dependent on exports for growth. And that’s put Beijing under rising pressure from trade partners to address its yawning surplus, which is on pace to hit a new high this year in excess of the US$1.2 trillion recorded in 2025.

The European Union is preparing to create new powers that could allow it to shut off China’s access to its single market as part of a dramatic new push to rebalance bilateral trade.

Meanwhile, foreign leaders have called on Beijing to allow for more appreciation in the Chinese currency, which they say is undervalued and gives the nation’s exporters an unfair competitive advantage. The International Monetary Fund estimates the yuan’s undervaluation in the range of 17.3% to 25.3% in 2026, with a midpoint of 21.3%.

“Overall, the latest data suggest growth momentum improved towards the end of the third quarter,” said Zhou Hao, chief economist at Guotai Junan. “While the property downturn and soft domestic demand remain challenging, stronger-than-expected GDP and retail sales figures, firmer manufacturing activity, and an improving labour market point to a more constructive outlook for this quarter.”

title: ECB’s Sleijpen says window is closing to limit warming impact
article:
(Oct 19): European Central Bank (ECB) Governing Council member Olaf Sleijpen said that the chance to limit global warming to the limit envisaged by the Paris Agreement is almost spent.

“Scientific evidence shows that the remaining carbon budget consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5°C is now almost exhausted,” Sleijpen said in Manila on Monday. “We are no longer choosing between success and failure, but between an outcome that is bad but still manageable, and an outcome that we can no longer manage.”

Sleijpen spoke in his capacity as chair of the Network for Greening the Financial System, a club of global monetary authorities. He also heads the Dutch central bank.

title: Japan PM Takaichi denies she’s driving weak yen, high rates
article:
(Oct 19): Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi strongly denied the notion that she’s responsible for a weak yen and high interest rates.

“Up until now, I’ve been criticised a lot for things like ‘Takaichi’s weak yen’ and ‘Takaichi’s high interest rates’,” she said in parliament on Monday. “I categorically reject those claims.”

Her administration aims to boost confidence in the yen by building a strong economy and achieving fiscal sustainability, Takaichi said, adding that that she will appropriately control the issuance of Japanese government bonds in next fiscal year’s budget.

The premier’s comments come as her year-old administration tries to ease persistent market unease about its fiscal management. Earlier this year, drafts of an annual economic policy blueprint fuelled concerns that the government was shifting towards a more expansionary stance, sending the yen lower versus the dollar and long-term sovereign debt yields higher.

However, Growth Strategy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said in September that Japan no longer needs a reflationary policy of aggressive monetary easing and fiscal spending. Takaichi made similar remarks earlier this month. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has said Takaichi isn’t a reflationist, a label the prime minister has long been associated with.

Market participants are paying close attention to how the government will fund a planned sales tax cut on food and higher defence spending without worsening the nation’s debt burden.

See also: Ueda ‘can’t tolerate’ underlying inflation further over 2%

Separately, Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor Kazuo Ueda, who appeared with Takaichi in parliament, said underlying inflation is rising very close to the bank’s 2% target. The governor also said that long-term bond yields may rise if the market perceives that the BOJ is not raising the benchmark policy interest rate at an appropriate pace.

title: Meta says Claude AI tool triggered No Kings Instagram suspension
article:
(Oct 19): Meta Platforms Inc said an automated security system mistakenly suspended the Instagram account of the No Kings Coalition at the height of a nationwide series of demonstrations.

The technology company offered an apology and a more detailed explanation for the disruption, which came during the group’s early-voting push ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.

Instagram’s engineering team found that the accounts’ “reading” activity triggered the security system. A tool from Anthropic PBC’s Claude was accessing profiles, posts and hashtags at roughly four times the normal rate in intense bursts Saturday, Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications wrote in a social media post Sunday.

“These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems,” Stone said.

Meta said an automated review about an hour later determined the account shouldn’t have been removed and restored it, though it took longer to return administrative access.

“We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error,” Stone said.

See also: China’s CXMT swings to profit after memory chip prices surge

The No Kings Coalition, an anti-Trump group, said Saturday that its Instagram page was unavailable for about 90 minutes and that organisers remained locked out of the account even after it became publicly visible again. Full access was restored at 5:33pm New York time on Saturday, according to the coalition.

Organisers criticised Meta for restricting the account during the demonstrations, saying Instagram was a crucial platform for communicating with supporters.

The coalition said millions of people participated in nearly 3,000 events in all 50 states and Washington in an effort to expand early vote access and defend election integrity.

See also: Apple iPhone Duo orders slip into 2027 amid pre-order frenzy

Stone’s statement on Sunday didn’t specify which Claude tool was involved, who was operating it or what activity it had been carrying out in connection with the account. No Kings did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The explanation clarified Meta’s initial account of the incident. Stone said Saturday that unusually high rates of posting, sharing or commenting had triggered the company’s automated systems and that such activity had caused the No Kings account to be suspended. He called the action “clearly” an error.

No Kings, which has organised several anti-Trump protests since he was inaugurated, said it plans a national organising call Wednesday focused on turnout ahead of Election Day.

title: CPA Australia prepares future-ready accounting and finance leaders
article:
Like most other vocations, accounting and finance are being reshaped by technology. Coupled with expanded business responsibilities and changing workforce needs, the skills essential for success are quickly evolving.

According to some CPA Australia members, accounting and finance professionals are expected to not just be bookkeepers, but also strategic advisors to organisations.

Lee Soon Wee CPA (Aust.), group financial controller at global offshore and marine giant, Seatrium, says that the growing adoption of AI and automation is accelerating this shift, with technology complementing human expertise and enabling finance teams to focus on creating long-term value for the business.

“Today, finance teams are increasingly relied upon to provide deeper insights, strengthen governance and support decision-making for stakeholders, including senior management and investors,” shares Lee. “With routine activities increasingly automated with AI adoption, finance professionals can devote more time to higher-value work such as forecasting, risk management, performance analysis and supporting strategic business decisions.”

Echoing similar observations, Ayo Canlas CPA (Aust.), CFO of SharkNinja APAC, says that accountants are asked to deliver greater value to their organisations.

“I am seeing a common thread where routine accounting tasks are now automated so that finance professionals can contribute not just from a finance point of view, but also towards commercial insights as well,” points out Canlas.

Technical knowledge in accounting is not enough to excel in the contemporary business world.

According to the Future of Jobs 2025 report by the World Economic Forum (WEF), employers expect technological advancements in areas such as AI and information processing, and robotics and automation, to be “transformative”, with nearly two-fifths of workers’ skills to become outdated between 2025 and 2030.

Technology-related skills, in particular AI and big data, were ranked top of the fastest growing skills.

Meanwhile, analytical thinking was found to be the most sought-after core skill, with creative thinking, resilience, flexibility and agility, along with curiosity and lifelong learning, expected to become more important in the years to come.

For Canlas, accountants must be tech-savvy and able to leverage technology to free up time for higher-value work, including developing stronger business acumen and other critical skills.

“So how do you take advantage of that unique point of view? You can already see what's happening in the business through a financial lens. The next step is using those insights and take that us one or two steps forward, and contribute meaningfully to commercial discussions and strategic decision-making,” he shares.

As one of SharkNinja’s first few employees in Singapore, Canlas had to contribute to charting the regional growth of the company, which is outside the traditional accounting job scope.

“For example, management will ask how to use past financial data to develop a three-to-five-year plan,” he explains. “That's a good example of something that is beyond keeping the books.”

Meanwhile, Lee adds that emotional intelligence is another essential skill for business leaders.

“EQ is also quite an important factor in our day-to-day professional life. When you’re in the office, you have to interact with other people like your CEO, your board of directors, colleagues, among others.”

Highlighting the importance for accountants to have more than technical accounting skills to grow beyond their traditional role, Lee shares his experience on a merger and acquisition transaction where he was part of the negotiation team.

“Imagine an accountant sitting across the negotiation table; it is not a matter of reading from a script. You have to apply negotiation skills, interpersonal skills, and stay on top of what's going on around you,” he says.

“You have to read the other party’s body language, be mindful of what you say and how you say it. So, these are certain soft skills, beyond accounting that you need to be very mindful of.”

Beyond the comfort zone and textbook

As evidenced by their experiences, both Canlas and Lee went out of their way to take on responsibilities beyond traditional accounting to grow in their careers.

Starting out in audit, Lee contributed in other areas including commercial strategy and initiatives. These experiences provided him with opportunities to grow and excel.

“I got exposure to mergers and acquisitions. In particular, I experienced the merger between two of the largest shipyards in Singapore, Keppel Offshore and Marine and Sembcorp Marine, to establish Seatrium,” he says.

“These are learning opportunities that are not found in textbooks.”

Lee adds that Seatrium views AI as a tool that empowers employees to create greater value, and has deployed it across the firm’s corporate functions to augment employees' capabilities and improve productivity. Within finance, AI helps automate routine and time-intensive tasks, enabling teams to generate reports more efficiently and focus on higher-value work such as analysis, business partnering, risk management and strategic decision-making.

For a global business like Seatrium, operating across 15 countries, technology provides greater visibility and control across its operations, helping the company to improve efficiency, consistency and transparency, shares Lee.

Meanwhile, Canlas shares that he spearheads the AI and data team in SharkNinja. Through his efforts, data is now more accessible across departments, enabling wider collaboration with more in-depth evidence and analysis that drives better and comprehensive business decisions.

“The different teams I'm leading are also benefitting from the broader investment in AI, because they now see better the connections between finance, strategy, business planning and analytics,” he says.

“When we think about managing risks and opportunities, we're not constrained to just financial data. We can see the bigger picture.”

Canlas is guided by the mindset of being a “business leader first, functional leader second”. This means one should understand business priorities and apply technical and functional knowledge to fulfil those business priorities.

Lee adds, “As the profession continues to evolve along with technological developments, finance leaders will need to combine financial expertise, business acumen and digital capabilities to support better business outcomes."

The value of the CPA qualification

While both Canlas and Lee believe in the importance of on-the-job learning, they also value the training and rigour of the CPA Program in supporting finance professionals to advance their career aspirations.

"As technology and AI continue to reshape the profession, the CPA Program equips finance professionals with not only strong technical foundations, but also leadership, governance, digital finance, analytical thinking and problem-solving capabilities needed to thrive in an increasingly complex business environment," Lee elaborates.

“It also suggests a growth mindset and a certain level of discipline, as maintaining the designation requires one to fulfil the requisite hours of continuous professional development (CPD).”

Echoing his fellow CPA designation holder, Canlas says: “It’s a designation that helps to ensure that the fundamentals are strong. In that case, it’s been critical for our hiring especially for technical roles.

“CPA Australia’s focus on the skills and knowledge that matter most to the profession helps me achieve two objectives at once. While supporting my team to meet their CPD requirements, it also helps strengthen their commercial mindset and broader business acumen.”

Another much appreciated aspect of becoming a CPA is the mentorship and broader career opportunities provided by CPA Australia.

“You get insights from mentors who share their real-world experiences,” says Lee.

He also adds that global recognition of the CPA designation opens doors for members to pursue overseas career opportunities and gain valuable international perspectives.

To Canlas, events and workshops organised by the Singapore Division not only provide professional training, but they also facilitate networking, allowing members to exchange insights and explore potential opportunities.

With many members becoming finance leaders or working beyond traditional accounting functions in areas such as sustainability, technology, banking, consulting, risk management and executive leadership, both Canlas and Lee agree that the CPA qualification is a stepping stone for accountants and finance professionals aspiring to elevate their careers to new heights.

“It's a designation that brings a lot of pride, but with that, it's also a lot of responsibility,” says Canlas.

Lee notes that the CPA designation is a signifier of a qualified finance professional.

“Professional qualifications such as CPA Australia provide a strong indication of an individual's technical expertise, professional rigour and commitment to continuous learning, all of which are valuable qualities when assessing candidates.”
